title: Do You Think Francis Ford Coppola Still Got It?

commenti.body: [removed]

I really like both Twixt and Tetro. Late Coppola is severely underrated. I think one of the big issues with Coppola is that his artistic interests (since maybe Rumble Fish) are different than what people want him to be making, so there's a constant sense of disappointment among audiences who want another Godfather, or Apocalypse Now. His more expressionist works are very good, sometimes great, but they alienate his audience. Megalopolis will be good, but it will probably be a massive box office bomb and a critical disaster.

Different audience today 

I love his work and I think he should be in the discussion for a spot on the Mt. Rushmore of directors. But like I said different audience today. Short attention spans, wants everything explained to them, and care more about representation then the actually quality of the film

I’m really excited for it and I think the promo pic looks distinct and has a clear style about it. This film will have a clear vision - you can like or dislike that vision but I think it will feel refreshing having such a distinct marksman’s feel to it. So often in mainstream cinema over the last decade it has felt made by committee so this I think will get praise for having a strong sense of direction.

Whether or not it’s a box office flop I think is irrelevant. Something like the Fabelmans didn’t do well at the box office but is still highly regarded and it’s gonna grow a following over time. I can see this being similar. I could also see it being a surprise hit too as cinema going habits return and people crave great stories

Coppola is a gambler. He gambled on both Godfather movies, gambled on Apocalypse Now, and gambled on One From the Heart. People think he lost his touch, but the very simple reason his movies failed (financially and sometimes critically) is because his luck ran out. Not to say that he lacked talent or didn't have an audacious vision, but when you gamble every single time, eventually your luck will run out. And don't take it from me, take it from him. He's the one who says the closer a project verges on failure the more incredible the end product will be if they manage to pull it off. 

IF

He's also said that the more he makes his movies closer to a dream, the more timeless they'll be. The same way that Apocalypse Now, 2001, Fantasia, and It's a Wonderful Life invite people to keep coming back for more, he wishes for his own movie to do the same.

All this to say that I highly anticipate his next movie and hope that his ambition and gambling pay off, because if they do, we'll have an all timer.

Yeah, Twixt is a masterpiece but it will be lost on most people. I'm always surprised how little people speak of Dracula too.

It's a bit like Scorsese, they want to be auteurs who don't bend, and sometimes it means doing small budget movies. Twixt was *so good* because of its limited budget. There this atmosphere of every detail behind catered for, no fluff, no grandiose effects, and even the way he deals with the clunkiness of the requisites is like clockwork precision. In the category of films of that budget, it's so great. It's like he wanted to go back to this scale and be challenged again.

Even his biggest bomb One From The Heart that set him back financially by 20 years is for me among his best. It's a down on your luck story of a tough relationship played out on a giant town that's entirely a sound stage and comes alive to echo the feelings of the characters. It's a great movie although it has that darker streak in the characters Coppola regularly does so it failed as a musical. He has so many interesting ideas in his films and I love how he often doesn't care for audience expectations he just goes ahead and makes the movie. Even Godfather III which was basically just a paycheck he makes the film a good bookend to the Godfather saga narratively speaking, despite everyone's criticisms of the acting and absences of characters. It's about the end of a fundamentally sad mafia don's life, still underneath it all the man who started in The Godfather as the only moral dude in the family, coming to terms with the fact that he turned out the worst of all of them, and nobody is there to save him.

It's tough for me as a lover of that era of filmmaking to try to talk friends into watching these, and then usually they are dismissed because they don't fall into those easy prepackaged intensely focus-grouped movies Hollywood puts out nowadays. Why can't people enjoy something that challenges you a little as a viewer and shows you something different of life? Why are audiences only interested in the disposable, forgettable, and barely a notch above average movies Hollywood pumps out nowadays? Really hurts me to see Hollywood and modern culture with the internet has conditioned so many out of these wonderful movies. They just won't enjoy them because it doesn't conform to the tiktok culture we're all in now.

I think it will be an interesting/beautiful mess. I think it will be a box office bomb, but it will garner a lot of attention, maybe even for awards season. He's pouring a lot of his own money, and (potentially) the last few years of his life into this. Its a passion project. Whether or not it's blind passion or inspired passion remains to be seen. I'm hoping for the latter and I'm rooting for him!

Coppola said he took this thing Elia Kazan did with his movies, which was having a word to describe the core of a film.

The word for The Godfather, he said, is Succession. Apocalypse Now is Morality. The Conversation is Privacy.

Megalopolis is SINCERITY.

Perhaps I'm being too romantic for an answer that requieres reasoning, logic, etc. In way, when you aim for sincerity, you can't go wrong. Sure, your artistic choices, the way you deliver your themes, may divide an audience, but when you are sure with what you want to tell, if you are brave, if you commit to your work, if you are honest with yourself, then that's all there is.

Now I remember a piece from another interview which fits in here:

>“On one hand, you’re trying to aspire to really do something, and on the other hand, you’re not allowed to be pretentious. And finally, you say, ‘Fuck it! I don’t care if I’m pretentious or not pretentious, or if I’ve done it or I haven’t done it. All I know is that I am going to see this movie and that, for me, it has to have some answers. And by answers, I don’t mean just a punchline, answers on about 47 different levels.'”

I trust Megalopolis because I trust the man's passion + sincerity.

 I hope he'll give us a film rich in themes and emotions.

No. His last good film was released in 1986. I have great respect for Quentin Tarantino’s views on what he calls “old man films.” He vowed to retire before he started making them, but he started making them. Look at this cast list:

Adam Driver
Aubrey Plaza
Giancarlo Esposito
Laurence Fishburne
Chloe Fineman
Dustin Hoffman
Shia LaBeouf
Jason Schwartzman
Jon Voight
Talia Shire
D.B. Sweeney

This is a scattered dumpster fire. 

You want to cast a film with some of the most peculiar actors in Hollywood? Were OJ Simpson and Patty Hearst not available? FFC lost his magic after 1986.

He hasn't dropped a legit banger for quite a while now. If I had to guess though, I think Megalopolis will do quite well. Even if he doesn't ever drop another juggernaut the man's legacy is unassailable. That run of films through the 70's is just insane.

Hard to say he hasn’t made a movie in over a decade and has only made 3 in the last almost 30 years. I think a lot of his blunders has to do with expectations, I don’t think his latest movies were bad.

No I don't, neither does Scorcese, most of that group is LOOOOOOOONG gone past their prime.  They need to retire and let some new guns take over.  

I won't ever watch a new one of their films.

I'm with you here, most of what he made after One from the Heart was more or less on autopilot, he's rarely if ever put 100% into a movie since then and if he does for Megalopolis we're in for something really special

coppola is not a conformist. he never was one. he is one of the biggest rebels in filmmaking history. this is probably his last picture, who gives a shit what some douchebags from twitter and rotten tomatoes say. in 100 years no one will give a damn about them, their "receptions" will only be a bleep in history books, while coppola's films will live on, many of them re-appreciated and celebrated. megalopolis is my most anticipated film of 2024
Excellent write up. Do you know the source of his “dream/timeless” quote? I couldn’t find it on first Google.

I wish I could remember. I believe he's said it several times, and certainly during his recent interviews when he was first starting on Megalopolis. MAYBE it's also in his book Live Cinema, but I haven't been able to find it. I promise I'm not making it up lol.

Damn. I’ll be looking out for it. I know the feeling, though, there’s many directors whose quotes I remember from reading their books, interviews and watching BTS and if someone asked me to say which one, I’d draw a complete blank.

only part i disagree with is the fabelmans. i really dont see that having staying power. the most interesting thing about it is it being teh closest Speilberg has ever come to saying "this is what makes me tick" and him being one of the greatest directors of all time, seeing that vision is interesting. But i dont see it having much utility beyond Speilberg fans. And assuredly there will be Speilberg fans in the future, like I said he's one of the greatest directors ever, but I cant imagine there'll be enough to make Fabelmans a stone cold classic like say Saving Private Ryan or Jaws or Indiana Jones or Schindlers List or (I could go on listing all the amazing Speilberg movies but you get the idea)

I'm generally very forgiving, and I love Tetro, am honestly kind of baffled by how poorly it's received, so I should be the perfect person to watch Twixt... But I really couldn't enjoy it. Your comment makes me think I should give it another look.

Coppola has always been one of my favorites filmmakers, and if anything for the sheer audacity to take on he system in the 80s by putting everything on Zoetrope studios. One from the Heart is a great film as well, and ironically something similar, but far less inspired as Moulin Rouge was a huge success years later.


There was certainly a time where he was not as invested as he mostly worked as a director for hire to repay the debts (see Jack and Peggy Sue Got Married). 
But he still managed to squeeze worthwile films like Tucker and Gardens of Stone in the 80s.

Dracula was essentialy another paycheck movie, but he elevated the material thanks to the use of old school special effects from the silent era and the great costumes by Ekko Ishioka. 

And while George Lucas always told the media he wanted to make small Indipendent films after Star Wars (but never did), Coppola used the funds from his winery to make proper Indipendent work. 

I wasn't a fan of Twixt, but Youth without Youth and Tetro were great films and very different from anything else made in America at the time. 

Coppola has been thinking about Megalopolis since the 70s, and when I had the privilege of interviewing him in the early 2000 for the paper I worked for I asked him about it. 

This was before his comeback with Youth without Youth, and at the time he said he was too ambitious a project and it was something that he pretty much had abandoned at that point. 

I also read a very early draft of the script in the 90s, and while it came across a bit lacking (and with shades of 'The Fountainhead'), the sheer ambition was evident and I feel we're very lucky to be able to see the actual film. 

At this point in his career, Coppola couldn't care less about more financial success (though I don't doubt he wouldn't mind more money). 
His wine business is a safer enterprise which allowed him to experiment with filmmaking for the past two decades. 

People worrying it might flop or be snubbed by Twitter really puzzle me... I mean, who cares? 
This is most likely his swan song, so the only thing it matters is that it's going to be good. 
And while I'm not so sure that's going to be the case, I can safely say that it will be at least be interesting. 

And in the current cinematic landscape, that's more anyone can ask really...

I don’t think it’ll ever become as famous or acclaimed as his other films (almost impossible to be that big) but I do think in terms of film buffs it will gain a bigger following over time for the reasons you listed, almost like an epilogue to his famous films. 

I chose it because it was the first film I could think of recently from  an auteur from that era that flopped financially but is critically successful

it's a complete unknown. 'recent' form would suggest not. also 'passion projects' give me the shivers. too long in gestation can be a bad thing. But you have to think such a master has 'one more in him'. Coppola has perhaps the best run in modern film history under his belt in the 70s. I just hope it's interesting!
Hear hear. People put way too much stock in IMDb ratings and comments and general bullshit from AI-generated hot takes on social media.

I want to believe. He made some of the best films ever made during the 1970's with The Godfather, The Conversation, Godfather Part II and Apocalypse Now. But 2024 isn't the 1970s anymore. And his last proper good film was Dracula (1992), which even then isn't a perfect film and has one of the worst supporting performances in Keanu Reeves (made more obvious when acting alongside the great Gary Oldman as Dracula). We'll see. But my heart realistically says Megalopolis is going to be a critical and commercial flop and Ford Coppola is out of touch. I want to be wrong.

True about Lucas but also worth pointing out that Coppola made that comeback trilogy on the camera that Lucas developed with Sony (the HDW-F900) which was the first big push for Hollywood and feature films into the world of digital cinema, something both of them had been trying to accomplish in different ways since the 80's.  Coppola employed his old method that they used back on The Rain People of making the movie on the go, and achieved another of his goals: building a movie making van with all of the tools to produce a digital film onboard. There were plenty of other digital cameras available to use by then, but the F900 gives those three films that distinct, and I think very beautiful flat/2D/abstract look that you can see in the handful of other films made with that camera.

There's no question that Lucas has been a big part of new film technology. And incidentally I think Youth without Youth was the first movie shot on Cinealta that still felt very much like 35mm.

Coppola already had the infamous silver fish in the 80s and got a bit too obsessed on new technologies himself, something that also changed his style as actors were being directed from a different room.

It's funny Coppola was essentially Lucas mentor, and when they met Lucas was a lot more idealistic and very much against commercial filmmaking... 
He swore for years he would go back and shoot small films after Star Wars, but never got even close. 
Although to be fair he never really cared much for directing and being on set to begin with.

He’s made some true stinkers over the last decades. His last good film with a real touch was Dracula. Rainmaker was genre fare, could have been made by anybody, but it was decent too. He hasn’t made a great film since the 70s. 

The films in which he’s tried to recapture his past glory have all been supreme disappointments - maybe Tetro was his strongest effort. 

I saw Twixt at TIFF and it was abysmal, many walk outs (I promise virtually nobody else has seen it) 

Megalopolis is a scary proposition as a film lover. Of course I want it to succeed but his track record isn’t very good. He’s not Scorsese or Spielberg who can hit repeatedly. I really hope for a surprise there 🤞because maestro deserves a last hurrah

It's crazy to think thay the Godfather wasn't just a critically acclaimed film, but it was also a massive box office hit.
Same for The Last Picture Show and The French Connection... (To mention two contemporary of Coppola who were also part of The Directors Company).
 
It goes to show how much mainstream cinema has changed, as these films now would only play in the arthouse circuit and the average moviegoer would find them too slow and cerebral...

I'd say Twix was the only movie of his that left me cold. Youth without Youth and Tetro were imperfect, but very interesting nevertheless and closer to European Cinema than the average American movie of the time.

I honestly don't see Megalopolis financially making a big impact, but only because these kind of films are not big hits anymore.

But ultimately I don't think it really matters in the short term, even if it's a flop.
It will be ultimately part of his legacy, so we can only hope it's a movie worthy of it.

But even in the worst case scenario, it will at least be a very daring and interesting failure.
And such films should always be championed!

Yes, Youth Without Youth is a standout among those films, very beautiful photography.

The new Sam Wasson book on Coppola's work is fantastic, a lot of great info about him directing One From The Heart from another room like you mentioned. I liked the way he called it "electronic cinema". 

And spot on about George, he never was passionate about being a director, but I think he saw himself as a filmmaker and for all we know remains passionate about film, but has other overriding priorities. The two of them definitely inspired or contributed to one another's separate but similar vision, and I adore their handful of collaborations and admire how each of them pushed the medium and art form forward.

We have no way of knowing if he's still got the magic touch, but just the way he and Driver talk about Mega has me very excited. Even if they don't pull off a flawless classic, there is every indication they are attempting something ambitious to reach big audiences while maintaining an experimental sensibility we associate with arthouse fare and that is admirable. 

It's also all Coppola's money and completely outside the Hollywood system, so we're sure to get something fresh. Mark my words they will **HATE** it if this film is a hit with audiences because they have no control over it and it will force them to change their trajectory if only even a little.

Happy that he's back and it being a box office flop can be an opinion that exist in the same person. The actual quality and the performance, especially in today's climate, are two different things. I will see it no matter what because I love taking risks in art and at least trying something. I'd rather see something and be like okay it didn't hit the mark all the way but it was interesting forsure.

Interesting, I might check the Sam Wasson book out.
I read the Peter Cowie Biography (which was very exhaustive), and at some point over 30 years ago I was even working on my own book on Coppola's career and the similarities with Welles.

He was very influenced by the live television movies of the 50s, and One from the Heart was his first attempt at doing something similar. 
He came from Theatre and was very much invested in actors, even fighting with Gordon Willis as he was too focused on them hitting their marks. 
The biggest criticism One from the Heart got was mostly about it was all style over substance. 
I disagree personally as I love the film, but it's true that he became a bit too obsessed on that with that movie. 

Unlike Scorsese, who had more of a philosophy of 'one for them, one for me' with the studios, Coppola was never afraid of taking huge risks and putting his own money on the line. 

Megalopolis is exciting specifically because it's another big gamble like Apocalypse now. 
Whatever the outcome, I don't see how you cannot root for the guy. 

It's obvious he's not doing this for awards or to get a big return on his investment. 

And Lucas and Coppola were also instrumental in getting funding for Kagemusha, something that was done purely out of admiration for Kurosawa.

These days you essentially have to double your budget when it comes to marketing. So even if a big distributor comes on board, it's very unlikely to get enough money allocated to make a significant debt.

So I think Coppola is not exactly expecting a box office hit. But the again, who cares about that?

This is kind of like The other side of the wind.. A real treat for cinema fans
[removed]
I totally agree with this
I could be wrong but I'm thinking he might have said it in an interview with either Esquire or GQ in 2021 (?). It was at least similar that he says.

The Wasson book mostly focuses on the making of Apocalypse Now and One From The Heart, and how those productions are exemplary of Coppola's mania and willingness to put it all on the line for his big vision. But there's a lot of good stuff in there about his entire life and how his personal experiences and lifestyle link to all of his films. The book was made in collaboration with FFC too.

Also love One From The Heart, hoping to see the new Reprise version in theaters soon. Perhaps it will get a warmer reaction with a new audience. 

I am thrilled that Megalopolis is finally happening. As you said, it's right in line with the big swing/big gamble method that has produced some of his most exciting work.

And yes, I love Kagemusha, there's a couple of good little featurettes on the Criterion release where they talk about their involvement. Also a big fan of Tucker, Mishima and the Qatsi films that they were involved in. The short documentary Filmmaker, made by Lucas, is a good look at a young Coppola in his element. And then there's Captain EO...definitely a part of film history, ha.

Nope, your initial impression was accurate. I remember actually being a little sad after watching. Kind of like seeing a legendary athlete scrounge for minutes on a shitty team far past his prime. Hopefully he can conjure some old magic with this one but I’m not holding my breath.

Larger question here, Do Artists ever really lose it? If so, how?

Coppolla is pretty unquestionably, an all time great who ran into massive financial difficulties and his films stopped being a huge deal, and he couldn't make what he wanted, but his skill, style, and ART was still very much there. 

Has anyone ever really LOST it?

Dracula was ridiculed on release. Keanu with that accent! Sunglasses in the 1890s!

But now, wowza, people recognize that Eiko Ishioka is a flat out genius, that the intense acting is a feature, not a bug, and that the grand style of the movie just wasn't in rhythm of the early 90s, but it works MUCH better with a distance. 

Dracula is great. Just great.

There’s a very legitimate possibility that Coppola only “had it” for a few movies. Much like Ridley Scott I think it might be more of those specific contexts that created great movies more than the director themselves.

Coppola had one great run from 1972 to 1979. Ridley made two great movies in Alien and Blade Runner than hasn’t really made a great movie since. 

Compare and contrast with the Coen Brother, or Marty. Who have only had a handful of misses.

How little people speak of Dracula? It is his most successful film in the box office after the godfather movies and probably his most known film after those and Apocalypse Now. Yeah, it has a mot of detractors but it is usually the movie that they mention when talking outside of his know best works, even if only because it's quite likely the only one that they watched (One from the heart only gets talked for historical purposes a la heaven's gate and while rumble fish gets a lot of love, the amount of people who have watched it are in the two digits). It is also the Dracula movie that people think of alongside the Bela Lugosi one.


There is definitely no little talk about it.

Only operating on pure instinct I think this will be his greatest film, and thereby in the conversation for greatest of all time.

NO REASON Megalopolis should work, which is exactly why it will
Dracula is beloved by anyone who loves camp and/or silent era movies

While films like that are a rare occurrence, we still get some mainstream stuff that's quite dense and challenging like Oppenheimer. The reason audiences gave that one a chance is because the studio actually marketed it like they gave a damn, which is the true rarity. 

IMO the problem today isn't that there aren't filmmakers who want to do fresh, original, risk-taking things with mass audiences in mind, but rather the bullheaded studio system that doesn't know how or care how to present them correctly (unless you have Nolan's track record of past franchise and spectacle).
I guess we'll have to agree to disagree, as I find the idea that Nolan's films are challenging rather ridicolous...

Coppola's last films were wonderful and so sincere. It seems to me that he said that these three ''student'' movies were preparatory work for Megalopolis . He refined his sense of cutting on these older works. He has been thinking about this project since his glorious period in the 70s. The budget, the casting, the preparation time are there. I think we can be very optimistic.

There's no chance that it'll make anywhere near the $120m+ budget, that this is even a topic when the film is self-funded is bizarre to me. You think an 84 year old cares about losing money on a passion project he's been working on for forty years?
[removed]

You bring up a good point with it being self funded. I sincerely doubt he'll be watching the box office returns hoping it makes enough to justify Megalopolis 2: Electric Boogaloo. The reason why I brought it up since it's a (imperfect) metric of eyes on the film and overall interest. That leads me to wonder if Coppola even cares about if people see it/are affected by the film, or if he's at a point in his life where he's just got to get this idea of a film out into the world.

His 00s run is more experimental (each in different ways). *Youth Without Youth* is the the best of them, and his last big swing at intellectual sci-fi, which is what I assume Megalopolis is but on a much larger stage. No matter what the film will end up being, but seeing an old master getting to make a huge scale work totally on his own terms is what gets me excited. That's what I'm rooting for.
It’s Spielberg

> That run of films through the 70's is just insane.

3 of those films can be argued for best film ever status

> than hasn’t really made a great movie since.

Thelma and Louise and Gladiator say hi
